passages.t: A king who reigns in righteousness
passages.happening:
‘Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule with justice’ (verse 1). ‘Each will be like a shelter from the wind, a refuge from the storm, like streams of water in a dry land, like the shadow of a great rock in an arid land’ (verse 2).

Then the eyes of those who see will no longer be closed, and the ears of those who hear will listen (verse 3). The rash will understand, and the stammering will speak clearly (verse 4). ‘No longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected’ (verse 5).

The fool speaks folly and plots evil; he leaves the hungry empty and the thirsty without drink (verse 6). The scoundrel plots to ruin the poor with lies, even when the needy have a just case (verse 7). ‘But a noble man makes honorable plans; he stands up for worthy causes’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 28 to 31 were full of woes against bad leadership and false trust. Chapter 32 answers with a picture of good leadership: a king and princes who shelter the weak instead of exploiting them.

Who is the king of verse 1? Interpreters give three main answers. Some take it as a picture of the kind of king Judah should have, perhaps with Hezekiah in view, who carried out reforms and trusted the LORD in the Assyrian crisis. Others read it as a promise of the coming king already announced in 9:6-7 and 11:1-5. Others see it as wisdom teaching about what righteous rule looks like, since verses 1 to 8 read much like Proverbs. These readings overlap, and many hold that a hope first voiced about the kings of Isaiah's day finds its full meaning only in the Messiah.

In a dry land, shade from the sun and a stream of water could mean life itself. Good rulers are like that for their people. The first hearers, who had seen fools honored and scoundrels respected, were promised a day when things would be called by their right names.
passages.later: A psalm prays for such a king: ‘Endow the king with Your justice, O God’ (Psalm 72:1). Proverbs says, ‘By justice a king brings stability to the land’ (Proverbs 29:4).
passages.asks: Good rulers are pictured as shade and water in a dry land. Ask whether the people under your care find you a shelter or a storm. And ask where fools are being called noble in your world, and whether you go along with it.

passages.t: Complacent women, and a harvest that fails
passages.happening:
‘Stand up, you complacent women; listen to me’ (verse 9). Listen, overconfident daughters. ‘In a little more than a year you will tremble, O secure ones. For the grape harvest will fail and the fruit harvest will not arrive’ (verse 10).

Shudder, you who live at ease; put sackcloth around your waists (verse 11). Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields and fruitful vines (verse 12), and for the land overgrown with thorns, and every house of merriment in the city of revelry (verse 13). The palace will be abandoned and the busy city deserted; the hill and the watchtower will become pasture for wild donkeys and flocks (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The warning speaks of a disaster in a little more than a year, affecting vineyards, fields, the palace and the busy city. Many connect it with the Assyrian invasion of 701 BC, when Sennacherib's armies devastated Judah's countryside and fortified towns. The exact timing is not stated, and the passage looks beyond any single campaign to a longer desolation.

The women addressed are the well-off of Jerusalem, secure and at ease. Women often led the mourning in Israel, and Isaiah calls them to take up mourning now, before the disaster, by putting on sackcloth and beating their breasts, the ordinary rites of grief. As in chapter 3, the word is to the comfortable of the city, who are as much at fault as the men of their class. It is not a word about women as such.
passages.later: Amos speaks to the same complacency: ‘Woe to those at ease in Zion and those secure on Mount Samaria’ (Amos 6:1).
passages.asks: Isaiah calls the secure to mourn before the disaster comes. Ask what you are comfortable about that ought to grieve you. And ask what it would look like to take a warning seriously while life still seems safe.

passages.t: Until the Spirit is poured out
passages.happening:
The desolation lasts ‘until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high. Then the desert will be an orchard, and the orchard will seem like a forest’ (verse 15).

‘Then justice will inhabit the wilderness, and righteousness will dwell in the fertile field’ (verse 16). ‘The work of righteousness will be peace; the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever’ (verse 17). God's people will live in a peaceful place, in safe and secure places of rest (verse 18).

Though hail flattens the forest and the city sinks low (verse 19), happy are those who sow beside plenty of water and let their ox and donkey range freely (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The chapter repeats the book's familiar movement from judgment to renewal, but it names the agent of renewal more clearly than before: the Spirit poured out from on high. This looks back to the Spirit resting on the branch of Jesse in 11:1-2 and ahead to the Spirit poured out on Jacob's offspring in 44:3.

The renewal is not only of hearts but of the land and of society. Justice and righteousness come to live in the wilderness and the field, and the fruit of righteousness is peace and quiet trust, the very things Judah refused when it chose horses.

The first hearers, facing a ruined harvest, were promised a land so fruitful that farmers could sow freely and let their animals roam.
passages.later: Isaiah promises again, ‘I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants’ (Isaiah 44:3), and Joel, ‘I will pour out My Spirit on all people’ (Joel 2:28).
passages.asks: The fruit of righteousness is peace, and its service is quiet confidence. Ask where you are seeking peace without righteousness. And ask what it would mean to pray for the Spirit to be poured out on the dry places of your life and community.
